question.prompt:
A scanning code consists of a \(7 \times 7\) grid of squares, with some of its squares colored black and the rest colored white. There must be at least one square of each color in this grid of \(49\) squares.

A scanning code is called symmetric if its look does not change when the entire square is rotated by a multiple of \(90^{\circ}\) counterclockwise around its center, nor when it is reflected across a line joining opposite corners or a line joining midpoints of opposite sides.

What is the total number of possible symmetric scanning codes?

solutions.title: Color the groups forced by symmetry
solutions.explanation:
Squares that can be carried to one another by the required rotations or reflections must have the same color. We need to count these groups of squares.

Label each square by the coordinates \((x,y)\) of its center, with the central square at \((0,0)\) and adjacent centers one unit apart. Both coordinates range from \(-3\) to \(3\).

Reflections in the horizontal and vertical center lines can change the signs of the coordinates, and reflection in a diagonal can swap the coordinates. Thus every square can be moved to a representative \((u,v)\) satisfying
\[
0\le v\le u\le3.
\]
All required rotations and reflections preserve the two absolute coordinate values, possibly swapping them. Therefore two different representatives cannot belong to the same group, and every square belongs to exactly one of these groups.

For \(u=0,1,2,3\), there are respectively \(1,2,3,4\) choices of \(v\). Hence there are
\[
1+2+3+4=10
\]
independent groups.

Choose black or white for each group, then give that color to every square in the group. This produces a symmetric code, and every symmetric code is obtained uniquely this way. There are \(2^{10}\) choices. Exactly two use only one color, so the required count is
\[
2^{10}-2=1024-2=\boxed{1022},
\]
choice \(\text{B}\).
